Let’s explore Chapter 3: Class, Race, and the American Dream.
As the United States grew, so did this big promise—what we call the American Dream. It’s the idea that, no matter where you start, you can make it if you work hard enough. Sounds inspiring, right? But for so many people, that dream always felt just a little out of reach.
The truth is, class boundaries were real—sometimes even tougher than folks wanted to admit. After the Revolution, people argued about who should have a voice in government. And guess what? The answer usually came down to property and respectability. If you didn’t own land, your voice just didn’t count. Leaders worried that giving power to the “rabble”—their word for the poor—might shake up the social order. So, they made the rules to keep things just as they liked it, with power in the hands of a select few.
Picture a young man, full of hope, ready to work hard and get ahead. He might save every penny, but still run into invisible walls. The best land? Already snapped up. The best jobs? Reserved for people with the right connections. For a lucky few, meritocracy—rising by your own effort—was real. But for most folks, it was just a mirage.
When the Civil War ended, everything changed... and yet, so much stayed the same. Slavery was over, but class lines didn’t just disappear. In the South, poor whites and newly freed Black people found themselves fighting for the same scraps—jobs, land, any sense of security. And the folks at the top? They took advantage, stoking fears and resentments to keep everyone divided.
The way people talked about class got even trickier—now it was all tied up with race and identity. Sometimes, poor whites were pointed to as proof that race alone couldn’t guarantee success. Other times, they were used as a warning: see what happens if you don’t work hard or improve yourself?
Up North, industrialization meant big changes. Factories opened up new jobs, but those jobs came with long hours and lousy pay. Many workers were immigrants, and they heard the same old insults—“trash,” “scum,” “riffraff.” It didn’t seem to matter where you came from; if you were on the bottom, you were always at risk of being shoved further down.
Still, the myth of a classless America hung on. People wanted to believe that anyone could make it if they just tried hard enough. But the real story? The rules were hidden, and the odds were stacked against those without a head start.
So, as you think about the American Dream, remember—behind the inspiring words, there’s a complicated reality. For many, the path was anything but fair.
